utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning everyone. May we have today's appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Drasko. You may resume your seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And before I invite Mr. Cvijetic to resume his cross-examination, I remind you you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Drasko.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Cvijetic, and colleague, because I'm also a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Before we resume, there's something interpreters asked us to ask you. Please make a pause before answering a question and be close to the mic so that we can hear the answer and let us not overlap. Thank you. We -- yesterday I was showing you -- I was about to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's P633.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, you certainly know that Visegrad SJB belongs to Trebinje CSB; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: One can see that in the heading of this document. This is a short review of the military and security situation in the Serbian municipality of Visegrad. This overview was drafted in the Visegrad SJB. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let us now move to the relevant part of the document, which can be found on the following -- on the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in English, most probably, it's page 3. So in the Serbian version, it's the following - yes, this one - and if we could enlarge the last paragraph on that page. On both pages it's in the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So, please, take a look at this last paragraph. It is stated there that from the very first days when the town was liberated, the Visegrad Public Security Station has functioned. Its senior officers were appointed by the War Presidency of Visegrad municipality. And then it states that the station was manned with personnel from the area, that is to say, former MUP employees and so on. Mr. Drasko, in relation to what we've discussed yesterday in relation to this proposal regarding your appointment, we can see here - and can you please confirm this - that local authorities were rather involved in the personnel policy, not only in the prosecutor's office but also in the SJBs. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would object to this question. For one thing, this document is dated July 1992, before this witness came to Visegrad, long before he came to Visegrad. And, secondly, the Defence is asking this witness to comment on personnel issues with regard to the police which, of course, there's no foundation for, at least established at this point, how this witness knows how police officers were appointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness confirmed what's stated in the document. He obviously is aware of this role of the local authorities. He lived in the municipality in question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no doubt that, at the time, attempts were made to create the rule of law, and that is why, at the time of my arrival and before, I know that in Tasovcici, in Bileca, Trebinje, and Visegrad, there were efforts to create the rule of law and to have the government function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the -- this is another example of a broad pattern of what was going on. But how does it assist us in terms of the issues with which this trial are concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the course of the proceedings so far, you have certainly observed that Defence case involves that during 1992 many appointments in SJBs were made by the Crisis Staffs, War Commissioners offices, and other local authorities. This question of mine is important because it shows de jure and de facto control over such stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is exactly the objection I'm raising. This document is dated July 1992; it's talking about events in Visegrad early on in the conflict; and this witness is really not in a position to comment on it. To show this witness a document that I assume the witness has never seen before and ask him to comment on something that occurred before he even showed up in the municipality is just not an appropriate line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And the document, for whatever use can be made of it, speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. And it's been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please, let's move on, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, do you know that the local public security station with which you probably cooperated had personnel problems because they were, according to the systematisation or establishment of posts, they were short-staffed, also because of possible involvement of police officers in the fighting and the war?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon arrival in Visegrad, I realised that not only they were short-staffed but that they don't even have enough fighters to defend the area that was in between Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde. Many people deserted the ranks. One can see that from criminal reports I drafted at certain points in time there were not more than 150 men at the front lines. Now I don't know about the police, so -- but the police was forced to strengthen the lines. Many policemen also got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes. You anticipated my following question. Namely, my learned friend, Mr. Olmsted, showed you a list of police members from the month of October. And we noticed that at the time already four of them had been killed, which is a confirmation of what you just told us. But to finish with this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Penultimate paragraph, Mr. Drasko. Could you please find the sentence where 2000 is numbered. It is stated here that: "Through the activity of the Red Cross, over 2.000 Muslims were moved out in an organised manner from the area of the municipality." Now, I would like to remind you that this was done under the organisation of the municipal organs. Can you confirm that the Red Cross was also involved?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard this from late Baton [phoen]. I can't remember his surname at the moment. That's how people used to call him, Baton. Namely, that they were organising convoys for the movement of civilian population out of the town. I don't know how many people left, but I know that from Capljina, where I used to live, not a person could leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But my question to you was whether you know whether Red Cross was involved in these activities.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I want to show another document to the witness, already in evidence; P158, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please switch off his microphone when not using it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, did you hear the request to switch off your microphone when you aren't using it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, this is a report or information on the work of the Trebinje CSB from 1st of July to 15th of August, 1992. I would like to draw your attention to the following page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the following page. I assume, then, the following -- this is just a certificate stamp. Yes, the following page in the Serbian version. It's this paragraph which starts with the words: "Special programme" -- "special problem." In the English version, it's non-functional communication system. Let me just check if we are on the right page. Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, this information, as we've discussed just now, the chief of the CSB was Mr. Krsto Savic, and here they are enumerating some of their problems: short-staffing -- short-staffed, you mentioned that; then the problems with the communications; lack of equipment; shortages of fuel that are very common; and breakup of communication because of which we are not even now able of processing the information from old Herzegovina. In the document which was actually a proposal for your appointment, it is stated, and I pointed that out to you, that the proposal should be sent using radio communications. The document I've shown you before this one, namely, the report on some security problems in the area, it was stated that a courier should be used. Now, this is what I want to ask you: Geographically speaking, was Visegrad physically connected to Trebinje in such a way that one could stay within the Republika Srpska territory?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We needed to go through Priboj and Podgorica, me and my family. And when we were on our way to Sarajevo, we had to go through Sjemac. Through Sjemac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Hold on a second. We have to wait for the interpreters. So you were saying you went through the territory of --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbia. Priboj and Uzice we travelled by train, and then by bus to Trebinje. When I was in Sarajevo to make my pledge of allegiance, I had to cross the Sjemac mountain. This road goes via Rogatica. Since there were constant sabotage actions along that route, on one occasion, when I was travelling with Colonel Luka Dragicevic, he gave me his rifle and he told me, Listen, if Muslims are about to capture me, kill me. Don't let them get me alive. The communication was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You answered my question in your last sentence, so I won't repeat it. You mentioned the oath you had to make. That's an oath that has to be made by judges and prosecutors; right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now go to the very end of this document. In the Serbian version, the paragraph begins on the previous page. Could we please go back to that page. In the English version, it's also the last paragraph. I don't know if we have it, but we should see it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, this report says the following: "For the well-known reasons of the non-functioning of judiciary organs in this area, reports were not filed in a timely fashion, although most of the cases have been processed and completed, which will be done very soon." And then the author of the report adds that a -- an additional difficulty with the completing of criminal reports is the fact that the perpetrators are impossible to identify, and it's also impossible to apprehend and interrogate the individuals who have taken part in the commitment of those crimes. Now, I would like to know about your experiences in the year 1992. One of the basic problems in your work was the inability to reach both the victims and the perpetrators of the crimes, in order to do the work required; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, the last part that you read out from the document, does that also appear in the English translation? And the reason I'm asking is that the paragraph -- the penultimate paragraph seems to suggest that, in the last sentence, that 28 reports were registered against identified perpetrators; whereas, nine of the reports were against unknown perpetrators. This would seem to suggest that, in fact, by far the majority of the reports that were filed were against identified perpetrators. So I'm just confused about the apparent inconsistence between the two parts of the evidence that you have shown us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a known perpetrator can also be outside of the reach of the law enforcement bodies. I was speaking about the impossibility to reach them physically, and the reasons are stated here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please switch off his microphone when he is not using it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Once again, Mr. Cvijetic, the interpreters are asking that you switch off your mic when you're not using it. Thanks. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I completely understood the reasons why you said it was impossible to physically apprehend the perpetrators. I can imagine what these reasons were, but what's -- what is the evidence that you are bringing out to this effect?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it may be best for me to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, the victims of criminal offences, the witnesses were persons that the police and the prosecutors often couldn't reach; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true to some extent because many perpetrators were volunteers who went to Serbia with their loot, and there were a great many of them. They hadn't come to fight but to loot. As soon as they were able to come by some goods and weapons, they would leave for Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do continue speaking about victims and witnesses too.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, as a prosecutor, worked on a case. A young man by the name of Mitrasinovic killed his father. The mother complained of him mistreating her. And when he came back from the front line, he met his father at home and shot him from a fire-arm. We put him in detention, and the police placed him in remand prison. While I was working on the case and drafting a -- a request for investigation, his brother came back from the front line armed with an automatic rifle. He entered our office, he pointed his fire-arm at me, and said, Let my brother go. He killed my father not yours. And I froze. I did understand that he hadn't come to kill me, and I was able to calm him down. And I said to him that he must leave my office immediately otherwise I would lock him up too. For a while he was pointing his rifle at me, and then he put it down and left, and I never saw the man again. This is an example of the situation we were in as prosecutors. We were always risking losing our lives. There was no judiciary police, there was no regular police to protect us, or the military police for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We'll get there, but we owed an answer to Judge Harhoff. Do answer the following question though: The victims of criminal offences and witnesses and now -- I'm -- now I'm referring to non-Serbs, Muslims, very often could not be reached because they were in a territory that didn't belong to the RS?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I only -- I was only able to find ten persons; all of them were in prison at Uzamnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So while working on criminal offences where the victims were non-Serbs, that is, Muslims, a problem was also procuring evidence if it involved the participation of witnesses who are relatives or whatever but Muslims?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is impossible to work when you have no idea of what happened and you have no information.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm objecting to this line of questioning because it seems purely hypothetical. I think the witness has stated during examination that there were no cases involving non-Serb victims that were reported by the police. So I'm not sure where this is leading us. This witness is simply speculating how hard it would be to investigate a crime against a non-Serb when there are none. So I'm not sure this is helpful evidence to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And if I may add, Mr. Cvijetic, I thought that your line of questioning was designed to explain to us why the perpetrators could not be apprehended or investigated. And so far, I'm -- I'm being presented with evidence to show that the focus really wasn't on the perpetrators, but, rather, on the victims, and since the victims had fled, you couldn't investigate. But -- but that's taking the whole story from behind, if I may say so. So where are we going?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the line of questioning about this is not yet finished; I have only just started. And I'll finish with a relevant topic, and that is the issue of war crimes and working on war crimes. I'm moving toward that topic, possibly in an unorthodox manner, but I'll get there relatively soon. And I will discuss it with this witness by showing him some documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's very good. I look forward to that. But may I add that I would have wished that you started with this issue rather than in the end because then we could have saved the time. Please move on and get to your point, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see Exhibit P166.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, let us take a look at the heading so we know what this is about before we go to the last page. This is a dispatch of the CSB of Trebinje which was sent out on the 9th October -- of October, 1992, and it was sent to the MUP of -- in Bijeljina to the Crime Prevention Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go to the last paragraph immediately. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This is the last paragraph. I don't know if you can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can enlarge it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, here, the chief of the centre points out problems in their work and in the uncovering of crimes; that is, the perpetrators thereof. He speaks about personnel shortage, the use of personnel at the front line, the impossibility to bring in persons that have some connection to crimes for interviewing, which is something we have just discussed, and he says: "For a longer time, judiciary bodies have not been functioning, military and regular prosecutor's offices and courts, and in some areas such as Visegrad, such a situation still persists." Of course, at the time when he was writing this. And on-site investigations were conducted in the absence of the investigating judge, the prosecutor, and so on. Furthermore, he goes on to speak about problems when military bodies are supposed to work on a crime. He says that they don't go to the site; whereas, the civilian police assists them in collecting evidence. Now, here's my question to you concerning these allegations: Mr. Drasko, the prosecution and processing of war crimes is in the jurisdiction of Military Prosecutor's Offices and the military judiciary in general; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In a situation when all able-bodied men in the territory covered by, let's say, the CSB of Trebinje and your municipality became conscripts, they came under the jurisdiction of military courts if they committed other crimes in that territory; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, then, won't you, when I say that the military judiciary bodies processed them even if they commit crimes against persons of other ethnicities, regardless of the nature of the crime?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, won't you, that this is the source of the problem? Because the military judiciary only started working in 1992, but from the point of view of manning and equipment, they were not able to work on such a large number of cases that now was in their jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I called military judges and prosecutors parade horses because they only paraded about but they didn't really do their job, although they were receiving their salaries from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let us continue discussing the topic of war crimes then. You will agree with me, won't you, when I say that for the processing of war crimes - now that we have clarified the matter of jurisdiction - it was necessary to create the required preconditions; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, won't you, when I say that one of the basic preconditions was that all three peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina understand and accept the fact that they must make it possible for a member -- for members of their people to be tried for the crimes they committed; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In addition to the fact that national consciousness had to come to its germination, another precondition was to make sure that the judicial system within a state has all the staff, all the expertise, and all the equipment necessary for processing crimes, such as war crimes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, you will agree with me, won't you, that it was necessary to have general safety preconditions in place, both for victims and witnesses and for law enforcement organs so that they can carry out their job without any bias and in a focussed manner; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blasko --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Drasko.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My apologies. You will agree with me, won't you, that in 1992, unlike in other war years, not one of these preconditions was in place for proper processing of war crimes; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in some larger military courts, prosecutors were conducting the processing of the case, and once encountering any of the problems mentioned before, such as inability to interview victims or witnesses, or could not do the technical, let's say, excavation of mass graves, they decided to suspend investigation until the conditions were available and ripe; are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I did in all of my cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And there was a practical reason behind that. Had the prosecutor been insistent in processing the cases, it could have happened that many of the perpetrators would have been found not guilty because of the lack of evidence?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The risks were obvious. Had they been acquitted, they would be under the non bis in idem principle. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me just repeat. These people could never be tried again; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Which was according to this principle of non bis in idem?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a case such as that in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you will agree with me, won't you, that in a situation like that it was more useful to document the criminal offences, to collect whatever evidence that's available at the time, and then wait for the conditions to be present for processing of criminal cases in question?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be the normal procedure. But all my criminal reports were dropped by Rajko Bojat [phoen] in Sarajevo because of lack of evidence, and the process was stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yet all the criminal offences remained live, and investigation could have been continued at any point?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the prosecutor's office in east Sarajevo does not wish to do so, it seems. They haven't done anything so far, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, your testimony is that investigations were given up because of the risk that the perpetrators would have been acquitted in case of a Prosecution because of the lack of evidence. Now, would you not, under such circumstances, ensure that at least a registration was made of the investigation and then a note that the investigation was temporarily suspended until such time as the investigations could be resumed? Do you know if such registrations or notes were made in each of these cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when I found out about this case, I informed the prosecutor of Bosnia-Herzegovina; the Prosecutor was Mr. Jucevic [phoen]. And cases -- and I copied all the files that I had with me and sent them to the court in question, which was done also by other lawyers. In Simsic case was Mr. Karkin, Fahrija and a prosecutor of Bosnia-Herzegovina - since they knew about the cases - was the body in charge of further processing them, especially when one is talking about, for instance, Jelesic case where the victims were children, and there were plenty of such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What nationality were the -- or what ethnicity were the children?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Serbs. I apologise, may I add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon my arrival in Visegrad, I was made aware of this case, but none of the investigative judges could go there because it was in the war zone, and only a misdemeanour judge went there, together with a film team. They made an on-site investigation. And upon his return, I helped him to file or draft a report. And this was only 30 days after the event itself. In other words, before my arrival, there hadn't been anyone there who could have made such a report on the on-site investigation, and the military prosecutors refused to go there. In my yearly report, I stated that in Serbia conditions are such that those who are afraid are glorified, and heros are being laughed at. Because this situation showed that if somebody dies on the front line, the military police -- the Military Prosecutor's Office do not go and conduct on-site investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, I failed to mention another condition that was necessary, namely, to have all the regulation within the state adjusted to processing war crimes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: For instance, at the time, in 1992, there was no law or act on protection of witnesses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Only with the reform of the judiciary in the 2000s things were organised in such a way -- or, rather, in a way that is organised before this Tribunal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Unfortunately, this is something that applies only to this Tribunal. It does not happen in such a way in Bosnia and Herzegovina. There, the witnesses are really at risk. The law you mentioned is only on paper, but it's not really being implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, let me round up this topic by giving you an example. You spoke about the facts that your wife was a prisoner in detention camp called Dretelj in the municipality of Capljina. Let's just make it clear: Geographically speaking, of course, this area was under the control of the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. At the time, it was -- this area was held jointly by Muslims and Croats. At the time they were together.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You told us that there, in the area under their control, there were 2- to 300 such centres for holding Serbs, some of them of private nature even. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this was also a privately held detention facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: With your permission, I would like to speak about what was being done in the camp of Dretelj. Namely, what I want to propose is that you decide whether we will discuss this issue on closed -- in closed session or in public session, because one can find that in your statement.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this is not relevant for this trial. There is a trial going on in Norway and in Sweden, and I -- I think that the perpetrators in that case who are neo-fascists should be tried in other countries, not only Norway and Sweden.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What I wanted to ask you really was when were such cases processed? How many years after the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Cvijetic, Mr. Olmsted is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. The witness is a prosecutor, and I think he thinks along the same lines as I do, on relevancy grounds. We're about to go into war crimes committed against Serbs and a case that involves this witness's spouse. It's tu quoque, it's not relevant to this case, and I think it's just not going to be a good use of cross-examination time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was about -- before Mr. Olmsted rose to intervene, I was about to observe, having regard to the witness's comment about relevance, that whereas matters of relevance are for the Bench and not the witness, this is, in my view, so painly [sic] irrelevant, Mr. Cvijetic, that you should desist. In other words, please move to a different line of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe you may have focussed on what the wife of this witness went through. But the essence of what I'm saying is this was -- these cases were not processed until this day by the organs of the Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, we'll move to a different topic. I only wanted to discuss the conditions necessary for processing of a case with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Drasko, you spoke about moving out of a Muslim population, about crimes during the direct examination. In one of the reports presented to us - and I think it was a military report - it was stated that the Serbian population was also moving out of the area. And what I'd like to hear from you is an answer to the question whether this was connected with the wartime operations, because I guess we'll agree that Visegrad was in the zone of the combat activities throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain. When my wife, myself, and the three children of ours came to Visegrad, I heard a story, according to which there was a judge and a doctor coming to Visegrad and everybody else moving out of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because I have a document with your signature on it, and, if necessary, I will show it. I hope you can confirm that you remember the document, in which you state that from 1990, in the area of Visegrad, inter-ethnic relations had been disturbed, which was reflected in the events described in this report signed by you, at least I assume, in March of 1993, and they refer to the events from 1990 till 1992. Do you remember the document?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote it, and there's no doubt that families from Uzice, Obrenovac, that is, relatives of Visegrad people who lived there, protested against the terror that prevailed after the election victory by the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that some people had been driven out. Which people?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: After the multi-party elections in that area, the SDA had the majority, certainly, because the ethnic makeup of the municipality was such. And then the Serbs, as the minority at the time, were being persecuted. Was that the subject of your report?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I have to raise a foundational objection again. This witness stated during his examination-in-chief that I think he said he was through Visegrad once prior to moving there in late August 1992. Now my learned friend is asking him a number of questions of what happened after the 1990 elections and the SDA power in the Visegrad before the conflict. I think there has to be at least a degree of foundation here before we proceed any further to establish where this witness is getting this information. Is he getting it from word on the street when he arrived in Visegrad, from literature that he read. I mean, we just don't have any foundation to establish that this witness can talk about this subject matter in a credible and helpful manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I had the impression though, Mr. Olmsted, that the foundation on which Mr. Cvijetic was relying was the witness's own report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, again, I mean, this witness was not in Visegrad until the end of August 1992, and we're talking about events that preceded that date significantly. So I'm not sure how this is -- this is going to be useful evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I tend to agree with you there. But the -- to the extent that Mr. Cvijetic is relying on the witness's report, such challenge as you have -- as you are able to make to the basis on which he came to those conclusions is a different issue than the immediate question as to whether Mr. Cvijetic can base his questions on the witness's report. And, Mr. Cvijetic, you would have gathered from my response to Mr. Olmsted that, to the extent that you're relying on this, it is only such of it as is relevant for our purposes, that we need hear about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, and that is, indeed, my intention. I will show the exhibit. It's Exhibit D034304.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, do you recognise the introduction of this document?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber how you made this chronological sequence of events from 1990 until 1992 in the Visegrad municipality, on what grounds? And you mentioned dates, names, and events here.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prosecutor Sahim Muhic and Ms. Tanaskovic were in charge of the investigation of these cases. Furthermore, it was well-known in all of Yugoslavia that Murat Sabanovic tried to blow up the dam on the Drina. Then there was the destruction of the statue erected to Ivo Andric. And then there were Croatian extremists and Muslim extremists who were killed in Hercegnovi. In Visegrad, Murat Sabanovic destroyed the statue erected to Ivo Andric. His brother, Avdija, was the vice-president of the SDA, and he was behind all that. In Visegrad, to establish law and order, the district attorney, Rato Ruljevac [phoen] I believe his name was, to do that -- one wanted to do that and went there, and the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina also wanted to establish peace there. The SDA had its plans called Brijest and Jelen. Those were like the plans of Fascist Germany. And the departure of Serbs from the town was an element of those plans. Even a fleet on the Drina was organised, consisting of armed vessels, and it was all about a system of arming and seizing power in the town. But it was prevented by the arrival of the Uzice Corps. Even then, tunnels were dug for them to be prevented to come. In April 1992, the units of the Uzice Corps entered Visegrad, and when they withdrew, the war started.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do confirm to me that you got all this information from official documents that you found in archives.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If necessary, I can show a police report which I have on me, but I haven't used it. It's from that period, and it's about the conduct of -- conduct of Murat Sabanovic. I can find it. It must be here somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We believe that you have it. Let me just ask you, on page 5 of the document, I would like to know how you got this information. You say here that the SJB - do listen to me, please - distributed weapons and ammunition to Muslim extremists and that's why all Serbs left the SJB in March 1992. The exact date is mentioned too. How did you get that information?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are documents to show that, official documents. And also we can see an order issued by the Visegrad Crisis Staff for Avdija Sabanovic to be tasked with establishing peace, and he takes charge of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Avdija Sabanovic, the brother of Murat Sabanovic, is tasked with establishing law and order. And police and law enforcement were duty-bound to obey him. I have the document here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So, basically, we're talking about Muslim extremists that -- who were the authority in Visegrad and who ran things there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found it here. This is a criminal report against Murat Sabanovic and Senad Kahriman, because on the 20th of September, 1992, they attacked police officers on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, you are proceeding in chronological order, and you mention incidents in which Serbs were victims; they were being killed. And they -- you also mentioned the incident where children were killed. Did you have official information about that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was some video footage, and Miroslav Kojic was -- was on site to investigate. There is a report about that. The footage was also shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, you are a civilian prosecutor, and you sent this document to the Military Prosecutor's Office at Sokolac because you believed that if some of these offences are war crimes, that they should be dealt with by the military prosecutor; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is about the general context of events from 1990 till the end of 1992. This context is dealt with by the indictment, and it was dealt with by the OTP in the pre-trial brief. This Trial Chamber, too, has adopted a package of adjudicated facts that have to do with the general context in the Visegrad municipality. In order to grasp the overall context and all events, I seek to tender this document as a Defence exhibit because the author of the document is present and has confirmed the authenticity and correctness of the allegations in the document. He signed it, and he stands by it. And this also is part of his perceived credibility as a witness because he fairly deals with the matter of war crimes and wartime events in the Visegrad municipality as viewed from both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The Prosecution would object to the admission of this -- this document. It's a -- a report to the state documentation centre for the investigation of war crimes against members of the Serbian People. By its very title, it's tu quoque. It's dealing with war crimes committed against Serb victims. The Prosecution is not challenging the idea that law enforcement and the judicial system were reporting war crimes committed against Serbs, and so this really isn't relevant to this case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, subject, of course, to the general rule of -- the overriding principle of relevance, isn't the rule that cross-examination is, at large, and as I understand Mr. Cvijetic's position, is that, whereas the contents of this document may, in their detail, relate to matters that do not counter what -- facts in which the Prosecution are relying, they are -- it is admissible because it is an item which would assist the Chamber in assessing the credibility of the witness. I believe that's a fair summary of Mr. Cvijetic's position. Mr. Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, if that is -- if that is the case, if it's for going to the credibility of the witness, of course, we wouldn't object on that grounds, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D333 [Realtime translation read in error "1D33"], Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure that cannot be 1D33, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is correct; it's 1D333.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I note the time. I believe it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yeah, I was going to suggest, whereas we're about two minutes early of the break, perhaps this is a convenient point. And I would remind you, Mr. Cvijetic, when we return, that, if I remember the Registry calculations correctly, you would have about 40 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the record, the Prosecution is now joined by Tom Hannis and Alex Demirdjian. And before the witness is escorted in, if I could just seek a clarification on the Trial Chamber's ruling on the last document that was admitted, 1D333. It is unclear to the Prosecution whether the Defence purports this document bolsters the testimony of the witness or challenges the witness's credibility. We're entitled to know this to determine whether the Defence sees this witness as telling the truth or to lack credibility. If it's for the purposes of enhancing his credibility, bolstering his credibility, then the relevance of it -- or the purpose of the document really is -- is not necessary because there is no challenge by the Prosecution at this point to the credibility of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course, in order to deal with the last part of your observation, Mr. Olmsted, the -- the Chamber's already ruled on the admissibility. In terms of the first part, I would have thought that this is something that you would deduce from the line of questions that the other side frames. And then, of course, to the extent that it has now been made an -- I shouldn't say be made an issue, to the extent that they are relying on it for such purposes as you may deduce, you do have a right to re-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I see your point. But we simply want to know whether the Defence challenge the credibility of this witness and whether that's the purpose of this document, is to challenge his credibility or to bolster it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic did say what he -- what his purpose was, and we had an understanding of it. And I don't know what your appreciation of it would be, but we'll see where we go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, we'll now finish with the last document I intend to show to you. Yesterday, in response to a question put to you by my learned colleague, you spoke about the kidnapping of either 17 or 18 Muslims, and you were also asked whether Republika Srpska authorities took any measures to clear up the events surrounding this criminal offence. Do you remember this question put to you by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. It's not a very clear recollection that I have of the question, but it's a well-known question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What you made certain in your response -- in response yesterday was that the kidnapping took place in Republika Serbia -- Republic of Serbia and that the victims were also citizens of Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The role of the organs of Republika Srpska in relation to that case would be only at the level of assistance in resolving the case?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I will show you a document now, 1D00-2433. I don't know whether you have the magnifying-glass still.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But you can still read. Now it's enlarged. Maybe it will be easier to read it now. This is a dispatch by the SJB Visegrad, dated 25th of October, 1992. You will also notice that in handwriting one can see the words: "Re: Dispatch link them together 26th of October." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have I read properly what's written in the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Visegrad and Rudo are the municipalities closest to the location where the crime took place; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Also, one can see from this dispatch that the Visegrad SJB is referring to a dispatch by the Ministry of the Interior, dated 25th of October, 1992, and that, for all practical purposes, they are just giving a response to the said dispatch - if you want, you can read it in the document - and in relation to the activities of the SJBs concerning these events; can we see this in this dispatch?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of the document, one can see that the minister of the interior was -- has shown personal interest in this case. And the chief of the SJB, Risto Perisic, mentions that in the bottom part of the dispatch. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Before showing you the next document, can you please tell me whether you were aware that the Visegrad SJB was involved in clearing up the case?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, based on this document, it was. Since, at the time, I was member of the army, the only thing I knew was that the army was also involved. At the relevant time, I read the dispatch sent by Colonel Ranko Kuljanin. I read it in the command of the Visegrad Brigade 2nd LPB. And in his dispatch he is asking them to try and clarify the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the issue of clearing up events surrounding this case was something that my learned colleague examined the witness about. The Prosecutor asked a specific answer whether anything was done to clear up the case, so that's, according to me, the relevance of this document. We have an answer to that question put by the Prosecutor, and I would like to tender this into evidence. And I also have a report regarding this very case because, on the very next day, some actions were taken following the dispatch. And I believe these two documents are really important, in relation to a serious crime, and I think this is sufficient foundation for tendering this and then the following document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, the only thing I can read on the English translation of this document is that it says that the Visegrad police station continues to carry out the operative activities in the investigation of the kidnapping but no Visegrad SJB members participated in this case. And the persons were not brought into the Visegrad SJB. That's basically what it says. Do you still think it's necessary to have this document admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the translation I heard -- I'm -- I may have misunderstood you. The dispatch here is stating that no Visegrad SJB members participated in this case, nor were the persons, persons who had perpetrated the crime, were brought in. And also it's stated that the case is being processed. But I'm trying to provide the complete picture; namely, this dispatch provides a foundation for the work of the SJB. And we will see that in the following document. This following document is a broader report about what has been achieved by that time. I cannot put both documents at the same time on the screen. I have to show them to you one by one and then ask them to be tendered. But I can ask for this document to be enter into evidence later on, once I've shown the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution doesn't object to this particular document coming into evidence as it certainly shows communication between the SJB Visegrad and the RS MUP. But having said that, this is probably not the appropriate witness to admit any more documents on this issue, because, as the witness has just said, he wasn't aware of any activities of the RS MUP or the SJB Visegrad in any investigation or reporting on this particular incident. So if it stops here and it's just this document, then the Prosecution has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's see -- let us see the other document before we take any position on whether or not to admit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please have 1D00-2769 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, you can see here --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which tab is this under?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under tab 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You can see here that two stations, Rudo and Visegrad, cooperated on this case, and that already by the 26th of October they had some initial information or indicia. It is obvious that it was not possible at the time to clear up the case completely, but they put into writing what they had. The event took place on 22nd of October, and already four days after the event this information was drafted. Can you see that, Mr. Drasko?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see from the document that they worked on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: From the document you can also see that through operative work and mainly by examining the bus driver, policemen obtained the present information and a description of the perpetrators and the events. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see the last part of the document. In the English version as well; we need the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The last sentence where it is stated that: "The ministry will be duly informed of all further information, measures, and activities which will be undertaken." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, if I -- I'd like to draw your attention to the date on the dispatch sent by the ministry, namely, the 25th of October; and then, on the 26th of October, we see that actions were taken. And I believe that shows that Republika Srpska organs took this as something of importance. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I see these documents for the first time only today.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have nothing to add in relation to tendering these documents. It's now upon you to reach your decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Again, the Prosecution raises the same objection, that this is not the appropriate witness to seek to tender and admit these documents. The witness has repeated now three times he has never seen these documents before; he knows nothing about any sort of work, operative or otherwise, on this case by SJB Visegrad or SJB Rudo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, what is your response to Mr. Olmsted's objection that the witness -- not having any connection with these documents? To the extent that they may be useful to you, they perhaps should be tendered through somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I must remind my colleague that it was he who started discussing the issue, who asked this witness whether he knows anything about the investigation, whether police was involved in the case in question. So now we have an answer to a question that the Prosecution put. And I think the issue is now closed thanks to these very documents, documents that are relevant, important for clearing up the case. I believe the conditions are there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, the witness's answers still remains: He doesn't know. That's exactly the Prosecution's point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In the Chamber's view, the documents are admissible but not through this witness. So they would be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit 1D334 and 1D335, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, thank you for your evidence. I have no more questions of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have finished with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We don't have questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, yesterday you recall we were looking at the Visegrad Prosecutor's Office KT log-book. And do you recall that the log-book showed that you received the first criminal reports from SJB Visegrad on the 9th of September, 1992? Do you recall seeing that in the log-book?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So from that date forward, you were performing the function of basic prosecutor in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certain activities. I did take certain measures, which means that the official authorities in Visegrad authorised me, although technically I wasn't yet elected; they authorised me to do what I was doing in order to prevent crimes and to establish the rule of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If the SJB --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it might be my knowledge of English, but in Serbian there is a significant difference between what witness said and what was recorded. I believe the witness says -- said --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me just ask him again and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: -- to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it goes -- the second part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just -- Mr. Drasko, if you could clarify the second part of your answer as far as your authority to act as prosecutor pending your formal appointment by the RS Assembly?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was completely familiar with the processes and the regulations because I'm a lawyer after all. And I was aware that my activities were temporary only. But in such a situation, I agreed to draft a request for an investigation because I expected that I would be elected once the -- once the investigating judge does everything he had to do, and that I would be in a position to write an indictment, which, indeed, happened. My -- the justification for acting this way, to my mind, was the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now we saw from the KT log-book that the SJB Visegrad filed three criminal reports with you in 1992. If the police had filed more criminal reports than three with your office, would they have been recorded in your log-books?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if they came acrossed [sic] a case where they could not identify the perpetrator and they filed with you an unknown perpetrator criminal report, would you have logged that into your KTN log-book?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Into the KTN log-book with entries about crimes committed by unknown perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if you received these criminal reports from the police, would you have taken it upon yourself, either as acting prosecutor or when you were formally appointed as the prosecutor, to take measures to pursue those cases through the criminal justice system?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly would have. I can give an example. In Gorazde, in ten years, I also worked on cases against Serbs for crimes committed against Muslims. It was the prosecutor's office of the Gorazde canton. I didn't actually -- I wasn't immediately involved, but I was chief prosecutor and I was familiar with the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: My learned friend, during his cross-examination, brought up this principle of non bis in idem. Did this principle prevent the police from filing criminal reports with the prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The Defence asked you some questions about the jurisdiction of the military courts, and I want to show you 65 ter 2003 -- or, I'm sorry, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just for the record, it has already been exhibited as P1287.07 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, are you familiar with this law?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And was this -- this law, which is entitled: "The Law on Military Courts," and it's from the SFRY, but is this the law that applied to the Republika Srpska in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 2 of both the B/C/S and the English and take a look at Article 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We can see from Article 13 that it enumerates the Articles under the SFRY Criminal Code and the circumstances under which the military court has jurisdiction over one of these crimes when they are committed by a civilian. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: For example, if we look at item number 4, it's citing Article 123; and it states that this is -- that: "The military court has jurisdiction over civilians who commit this crime if it is directed against servicemen or the destruction of property of greater value that is a part of the equipment owned by the armed forces of the SFRY." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could look at -- later on in this Article...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I think we have to turn the page in both the B/C/S and the English. And if we can zoom in on the last paragraph of Article 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, we see the last paragraph states: Military courts try prisoners of war for any committed criminal act and for crimes against humanity and international law (under Articles 141 through 146 of the Criminal Code [sic] of the SFRY). Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How do you interpret this provision?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that, we must establish who is to be considered a prisoner of war. Unfortunately, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, my wife, too, who was transferred from the medical centre, was considered a prisoner of war, just like medical doctors and others. In Visegrad, the army kept persons prisoner in military camps, although they were -- or, rather -- correction, in military prison although they were civilians. In Bosnia, people used to say -- speak about the exchange of prisoner of war, although they were civilians. So that regular citizens of Bosnian Serbs were considered prisoners of war even though they were not -- or, rather, because they were not organised so as to be able to flee in time. Most times they were not soldiers who put up resistance but, rather, civilians, regular people. That is unfortunate, but that is the reality I came to learn. That is why the treatment of prisoners of war were such. But --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, could you repeat your last sentence. And then let me ask a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about these offences where people were treated as prisoners of war and kept in prison. But later on, when proceedings were initiated against them, there was no evidence, and they were acquitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I just want to clarify something with regard to this particular Article of the Law on the Military Court. This paragraph we just read says the military courts can try prisoner of war; in other words, is this referring to POWs who are perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly, yes, perpetrators of criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If a civilian who is not a prisoner of war commits a war crime, then who had jurisdiction over that case?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speaking about humanitarian law, in that period I think military courts were supposed to try, before the war, under these laws and regulations, because these most serious crimes against the Geneva Conventions - and the reference is mentioned here - crimes against humanity and international law, are under the jurisdiction of military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this then: Where under this Article 13 is the military court given jurisdiction over civilians who commit war crimes where those civilians who are the perpetrators are not prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I must intervene. I think it will be useful to show the witness Article 9 of this law also, which provides for the basic jurisdiction of military courts. It has already been shown in this trial. And the article that my learned friend is dealing with is only expanding on that jurisdiction as outlined in Article 9. So it may be good if we could read out Article 9 because it states the personal principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, we can certainly look at Article 9, if we go back to the previous page. I'm not going to read it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But, Mr. Drasko, you can certainly take a look at it. Mr. Drasko, as I read Article 9, this specifies when a person is considered a member of the military. Is that how you read it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says here: A civilian -- or, rather, such a person shall be considered a civilian who, and under paragraph 1 of this Article, is not a serviceman or a prisoner of war. That is such -- to such a person that the provisions of this law are not applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I want to return to my original question. We've looked at --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We looked at Article 13. It specifies when the military court has jurisdiction over civilians. We looked at the provision that deals with war crimes, and it specifies that the court has -- military court has jurisdiction over war crimes committed by prisoners of war. My question to you is: On what basis, under this law, do military courts have jurisdiction over civilians who are not prisoners of war who have committed war crimes?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me ask the question again so it's clear. A civilian who commits a war crime but is not a POW, who has jurisdiction over those cases?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian courts. I think it's civilian courts. Because we're talking about civilians, so civilian courts have jurisdiction. But sometimes it's difficult because persons who didn't meet the conditions to be prisoners of war still were considered as such, and they were -- they were to be tried by military courts. But if it's established that they aren't really prisoners of war, then they should be tried by civilian courts as is now being done in Bosnia and Herzegovina, et cetera. My wife, in Norway, isn't considered a prisoner of war, even though she was considered to be one by the HOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Are you aware of any efforts, either by the military or the civilian police, in 1992, to investigate war crimes against non-Serbs. And let's just limit it to where you have knowledge to the Visegrad municipality.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meetings were held, and as a prosecutor who should launch pre-trial proceedings and initiate other activities to solve criminal offences, I invited the district prosecutor of east Sarajevo, Sajko Gojkovic [phoen] to these meetings; then the republican prosecutor, Miroslav Gladanac, I invited him to the meetings in writing; and the meetings were to be about war crimes and their resolution, among others. I invited the command of the brigade too, that is, military personnel, as well as civilian personnel from the SJB. And they all came to the meeting except for those from Sarajevo. We insisted that the issue of accountability for war crimes must be insisted upon. There was this Muslim by the name of Mutapcic [phoen]; there was case against him. And I wrote a criminal report -- or, rather, I wrote a report against the persons I suspected of having killed him. The reports went to the Military Prosecutor's Office in Bileca because he was a prisoner of war, and we processed this case later. The agreement reached at those meetings was that the law must be strictly implemented with regard to the protection of property and protection of people. But my fellow prosecutors didn't come to those meetings, and they said, Well, working on war crimes is your private affair.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to focus you on my question. I'm only talking about war crimes that were committed against non-Serbs. In other words, Muslims or Croats are the victims of the war crimes. In 1992, are you aware of any investigations by the police - military or civilian - of war crimes in which the victims were non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not aware that these crimes were investigated at all. I never received any criminal reports to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, we thank you for your attendance before the Tribunal. Are you now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home. The usher will escort you from the courtroom. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wish you much success in your work and that you may solve all war crimes cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, just two matters while we're waiting for the next witness. First, my apologies. I gave the wrong exhibit number for the Law -- the military courts; it's P1284.07. And, secondly, since Mr. Demirdjian is going to lead the next witness and I want him to occupy my chair, is it all right if I may be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Olmsted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. No preliminary matters. The next witness is ST-167, Mr. Dragan Raljic. No protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- I understand there's a ten-minute gap before the next witness comes, so we would rise and resume when he's available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare to say the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. I would begin by pointing out that the solemn declaration that you have just made does expose you to the pain of the penalty for perjury should you give misleading or untruthful evidence to this Tribunal. The first formal question that I have of you is to give us your name, your date of birth, and your ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Dragan Raljic. I was born on the 25th of December, 1967. I'm of Serbian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm an employee of the Ministry of the Interior, working in the police station Kotor Varos, in communication-related field. I'm a civil servant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And how long have you been so attached?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since 1st November, 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Have you testified previously, either before this Tribunal or before any of the courts in the countries that comprise the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the -- we -- we thank you for your assistance to the Tribunal and for your attendance as a witness. The procedure that is followed is that the side that calls you as a witness - in this case, the Prosecution - would begin by asking you questions, after which counsel for each of the accused have a right to ask you questions, arising out of -- generally arising out of your testimony in-chief. The Prosecution then has a right to re-examine you, arising out of the cross-examination, and the Chamber -- the Judges who comprise the Chamber may ask you questions on relevant issues relating to the matters with which the Tribunal is concerned. We -- the Prosecution has asked for two hours to conduct their examination-in-chief; counsel for Stanisic -- Mr. Stanisic, two hours; and counsel for Mr. Zupljanin, three hours. The ordinary sittings of the Tribunal - you are beginning in the middle of a working day - is from 9.00 in the morning until 1.45 in the afternoon, unless it's an afternoon session, which doesn't arise in your case. And within that day's sitting, the time is broken up into periods of no longer than an hour and a half so that the taping arrangements which this Tribunal follows to preserve its proceedings can be changed and so forth. Notwithstanding -- and the breaks are usually of 20-minutes' duration. Now, notwithstanding those breaks, if, for any reason, you are in distress or have a problem continuing, if would indicate that to the Chamber, we would, of course, accommodate you. We are starting unusually -- at an unusual time, so we -- your -- the first part of your testimony beginning now would go straight through until we rise for the day at 1.45. And then we would resume your tomorrow morning at 9.00. And with that, I would invite counsel for the Prosecution, Mr. Demirdjian, to begin his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Raljic. You already provided us your personal details, so I would like to go straight to your educational background. It is correct to say that you went to primary school in Kotor Varos until 1982?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
