utterances.text: And that you completed secondary school in 1986, studying, I believe, electrical mechanics; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Mechanical engineer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And recently, I believe in 2007, you completed junior college in management; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And if I go to your background, in terms of your military service, I think you completed that in 1987 as a radio and telegraph operator?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. When you joined the police, you told us earlier you joined the police on the 1st of November, 1990, in the SJB Kotor Varos. That was in the communications section; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Prior to joining the police, had you attended any police school?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would all the unnecessary microphones be switched off, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I think there was a problem with the microphones. Is it all right now? I'll assume it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You said you did not. However, it is correct that you followed a training upon joining the police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: I underwent some training that was organised by international police at the time. These were trainings that lasted several days only, related to human dignity and such issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And did you receive any training in relation to your line of work in communications at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just to complete on that chapter, you were also leading a radio club in Kotor Varos, and I assume this exposed you to all terms [sic] of radio devices?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That was radio club from Kotor Varos called Oblas.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, when you joined the police station in 1990, what was the position that you were assigned to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: I started working at the position that was, at the time, called radio telegraph operator, radio telephone operator, encoding operator. That was the full title.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in that position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Until, I think, 1995, after which a new organisation was applied, and the full complement of workers were obtained, four plus one, namely, and then I was -- I became head of the group.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Therefore, in 1992, throughout the year that is of interest to this case, you were an operator, as you explained, for radio telegraph, telephone, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you, in 1990, when you joined the section, did you have a chief at the time? A chief of communications; I apologise.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: No. At the time, there was no chief of communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And did you have co-workers in the communications section?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: There was another more experienced colleague, Miroslav Kalamanda, who was already employed at the time when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So in 1990 [Realtime transcript read in error "1992"] there were the two of you in the communications section?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: In 1992? My answer was in relation to 1990. In 1992, there were the two of us plus another worker that started working in July that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise. I did mean 1990. And up until -- well, during the years 1990 and 1991, who did you report to? Who was your chief?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: At the time when I started working in the police station, or -- as it was called, public security station, the chief of the station was Munir Kovacevic. And since mid-1991, Mr. Savo Tepic took up that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in terms of your line of work, who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: In the public security station, initially, chief Munir Kovacevic, and then later Savo Tepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise. What I meant is in your line of work in terms of communications who was your chief or your superior?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: According to our line of work, it was the CSB Banja Luka chief of department for encoding --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the name of the officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the name, could you please repeat the name of the CSB Banja Luka chief for the department.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: You asked me about the chief of the communications and encoding department. And his name was Rakovic, Dragan, Drago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you've told us that the chief of the police in the second half of 1991 was Savo Tepic. Again, in terms of mid-1991, who was the commander of the police station at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember for 1991. I think it may have been Bogdan Djurovic who was the commander. At least for a period of time. And then later, this position was filled in by a man whose name I cannot remember who was sort of a stout man, I think a Croat. And then after him, it was Dragan --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Again, could the witness repeat the surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't catch the last name of Dragan that you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Dragan Bojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. If you know, can you tell us whether -- what was the proportion of the employees in the public security station, in terms of ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: In the period of 1991, if we're still discussing 1991, the makeup was mixed. During that year, there were Serbs, Muslims, and Croats working for the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you mentioned to us that the commander eventually became Mr. Bojic. Do you remember when he became the commander of the police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: I think that was after the arrival of Savo Tepic and his appointment to the post of the chief of station. It was a few months after his arrival. I cannot be more precise. It may have been in early 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like to take you now to the year 1992. It is an established fact in this case that the takeover took place on the 11th of June of 1992. Were you in Kotor Varos at that point?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can you tell us, On -- on the -- in June 1992, in your section, how many staff members did you have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: In June of 1992, it was Kalamanda, Miroslav and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You told us that a third person joined. When did he join?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was in July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what was the name of the third operator?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Vujadin Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, When the takeover took place, were you in the -- I apologise, there seems to be an interpretation --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry. Line 52 -- I'm sorry, page 52, line 2. Oh, yeah, it was changed. The name of the person was mis -- misrecorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Misspelt. Okay. It is fine now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Let me go back to my question. In relation to the takeover, you were -- were you at -- were you in Kotor Varos when the takeover took place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Was there any indication that it was going to take place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Well, there were indicia that certain developments were about to occur. One could not exclude conflicts, but nobody to could tell whether there was going to be a takeover or maybe a conflict with the rise. But the situation was tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, can you explain to us, on the 11th of June, what you observed on that day, in terms of the takeover?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: What I observed: The town was full of people in uniforms, some in -- in SNA [as interpreted] uniforms or camouflage uniforms. People were taking up positions in various places in town. There were check-points. On that day, there were no conflicts or there wasn't any shooting. Everything was rather quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You told us that you noticed people in SMB uniforms or camouflage uniforms. What happened per se? How did the takeover take place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: I don't know specifically how. I only saw people at various locations in town. Now, how the takeover or establishment of check-points -- how did that really look, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, is this relevant in view of the Adjudicated Fact 519?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'm getting to the forces that were present, Your Honour, to specify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Raljic, could you tell us whether you were aware of which forces were present in town?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: At the time, I didn't know which forces were in town. As I've already stated, there were a lot of people in various uniforms, and I didn't know who was who.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In the police station itself, did you notice a presence of these people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did you come to learn who they were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes. With passage of time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If you could tell the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the 11th of June, so in the following day, the subsequent days, various uniformed people were coming to the police station. Some of them wore lighter coloured camouflage uniforms that I hadn't seen before, wearing hats with wider rims. Later on, I saw blue camouflage uniforms that were police uniforms. Again, uniforms I hadn't seen before that. Then there was the regular police. They were people in various other uniforms coming in olive drab or SMB and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we start with the group that you told us were in a lighter colour of uniform, did you come to learn who was their leader?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Initially I didn't know who they were because they were all mixed in groups. I never saw them lined up in formations, either of the three groups. But according to my information, I think it was the people who were headed by Slobodan Dubocanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And did you come to learn to which organisation this group belongs to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: No, I did not find out whom they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If I go to the second group of people you told us in blue camouflage uniform, that were police uniforms, can you tell us, if you know, who they were led by?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Ecim Ljuban and Zdravko Samardzija. I remember them because Zdravko I knew from before. And as for the other names, no, I didn't know what the names of their commanders were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And Mr. Ecim and Mr. Samardzija, do you know from to which unit they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: I used to see them in -- or wearing those uniforms, and I believe they were part of the special police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And the special police unit belonged to which municipality?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Special unit was not part of any municipality. It was under the Ministry of Interior. It was the special unit of the police, not a unit of any municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you say "the Ministry of Interior," which organisation in the Ministry of Interior did it belong to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Where were they stationed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: I don't know any specific one location. I think they were stationed at different locations in town. I don't know where they slept. One could see them all over the town. I don't know where they slept.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And do you know, on the 11th of June, where they came from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Prior to this takeover on the 11th of June, in the police station did there come a time when the employees were requested to sign a loyalty oath?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Were you present?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: I think I was, for at least one part of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber where did this take place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: In Kotor Varos retirement home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And who convened the meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember who convened the meeting, but it must have been senior officers of the station, either the chief or the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And who else was present?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: In addition to the senior officers of the SJB and all the uniformed personnel, I don't think there was anyone else present.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can you just tell us how this signing of the loyalty oath took place. What was -- what were you told?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact formulation of the statement that needed to be signed, but, in general, people were required to sign that they are willing to continue performing their duties under the aegis of the new-formed ministry. That was the basic formulation. I don't think there were any threats made that someone may lose a job. It's a form which you have to sign when you're moving to a different position, to a different organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just to be clear, when you say "the new-formed ministry," which ministry are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I think it was called at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And do you remember when this signing of the loyalty took place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: I can be a few days off, but, in general, it was maybe late April or May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, but a part -- part of witness's answer on page 55, 24, and page 56, 4, I saw it first in the -- in the transcript and then it was deleted and now it's not recorded. Because he gave the comment what -- what kind of a -- that -- something along the lines about loosing a job and all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think this should be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Raljic, when I was asking you about the signing of the loyalty oath, you explained to us what was told to you. And you said, in general terms: "People were required to sign ..." Can you continue there, because I think a part of the answer is missing.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: People were asked to sign that they will loyally continue performing the tasks that they were already conducting, and I'm not aware of anyone issuing threats to employees to the effect that they might loose their jobs should they not sign the document. I have not heard anyone say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, on that -- at that moment when you were asked to sign the loyalty oath, to your knowledge, did anyone decide not to sign it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: There was some discussion about that, who would sign it and who wouldn't. But the meeting didn't last long, maybe 20 minutes or half an hour. I can't really say now. Because the meeting was, in fact, forcibly interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, did some staff members stop showing at work after this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: I really cannot recall. It's possible, but I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, other than the senior staff of the SJB at this meeting, were there any other superior members of the higher echelons of the MUP present during this signing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the presence of anyone from the higher echelons. I don't think so. I doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, if we go back to the 11th of June, in relation to communications, what effect, if any -- if anything, did the takeover have on your work?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: The communications lines didn't function. Phone lines, teletype lines. Only radio communication was possible. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And how long did that last?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: At the moment when the lines were interrupted, this situation prevailed for about seven to ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And prior to the 11th of July, were all your communications functioning -- 11th of June; I apologise.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: After those initial seven to ten days, were you able to communicate and send dispatches?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Only occasionally because there were constant shortages of power, almost daily. Today we would have power; on the following day, not. And it went on like that all summer long. So the communications lines were unreliable, so we couldn't really be sure that we would be able to send a dispatch at any given moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, when you're saying that the lines were unreliable, I want to go back to those seven to ten days that you were talking about earlier. During those days, was there any damage to your equipment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what happened to the telephone lines between the initial seven to ten days?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: The telephone lines were not functional.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did you come to learn why they were not functioning?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: I never learned the real reason, whether there was an interruption somewhere, whether it was up to the post office, but I never really heard what the real reason was why the phone lines didn't function.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the equipment that you had in your section, can you tell us, first of all, if you kept the same equipment you had prior to the takeover?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes, we kept the same equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what sort of equipment did you have in the communications section?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: We had a regular phone line, a special dedicated phone line. We had teletype communications for sending out dispatches. And we also had a UHF radio communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And did you also have a machine for encryption purposes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now you just told us that after the 11th of July [sic] you had some problems in sending your dispatches; what was it that caused the problem? Was it your equipment; was it the lines? Could you tell us.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: The most important problem was the shortage in -- in electrical power. The teletype machine couldn't function without electricity. If we had no electricity, we couldn't send out dispatches. And if the other side, the recipient, didn't have electricity so they couldn't receive it, so there was no point in sending it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now the dispatches that you're talking about are those documents that you are typing in -- in the machine itself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: The -- we receive a typed dispatch which is signed, and then we type it into the teletype machine and send it out that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Demirdjian. I don't want to interrupt. But I think we need to clarify one thing. I noticed even before, during the -- the previous -- the two witnesses ago, that on some occasions the "UKT," UKT, was translated as "UHF" radio communications. I believe the "UHF" stands for "ultra high frequency." And actually what the witnesses are talking about are ultra short frequency communication. So just for the -- for the sake of clarity of the transcript, in the future, that we know what we are talking about. It should be stated in each and every answer UK KT. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Maybe this is something that Mr. Raljic can clarify for us when you're talking about the radio equipment.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes. UKT is the radio communication that we used, that's actually VHF; whereas UHF stands for higher frequencies over 400 megahertz. We worked on the frequency on 157.7 megahertz. That's actually VHF.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, during the periods of the day where you told us that the lines would be down, were you eventually able to send the dispatches that you were requested to send?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: From time to time, yes. When the system functioned, we were able to send out outgoing dispatches or possibly receive dispatches if there was electrical power.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in terms of electrical power, did you have a generator in the police station?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Later we did have a small generator, but we didn't use it at the communications centre. It was a small generator which we used for lighting and so on. But that was only later. If we had used a generator for the teletype machine alone, that wouldn't have helped us much because if there was no electricity supply in town, that is, if the phone exchange of the post office was without electricity, then it was no good again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Therefore, if the electricity is down, you told us that the only means left was the radio communication?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: There was radio communication. The duty officers -- officer could communicate in simplex radio communications without the mediation of a repeater because in such a situation the repeater couldn't function. There was an RU-210 radio station which could function if fed from a battery.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, this radio communication, what was the range? How far could you reach with this radio communication?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Well, VHF waves are specific, especially if you have a simplex radio network, that is, if you work without a repeater. Then the waves propagate in a straight line. But it depends on the configuration of terrain. Sometimes you wouldn't be able to communicate over 500 metres if there was a little in between or something. Or -- but, on the other hand, if there was optical visibility, you could communicate over a distance of ten or more kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the means of communications that were available to the chief of the police station, could you just tell what communications he had available in his office?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: The chief of the SJB has a regular telephone. I believe he also had a fax machine and a hand-held radio station, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in terms of telephone, are you referring to a special telephone, or was it a regular telephone line?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: The chief had a regular phone line with a number registered with the post office. And if he dialed 8 or 9, he could reach the exchange and then switch to the special or dedicated line.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did anybody else in the police station have a phone line like the police chief, registered at the post office?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: A phone line, yes. Such a phone line was also with the Deputy Commander, the chief of the crime service, the duty officer, and possibly the Deputy Commander [as interpreted], I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you told us about dialing 8 or 9 and reaching this special or dedicated line ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: While I'm asking the question, if we could display on the screen Exhibit P1471, which is tab 4 on the list that was provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Raljic, can you tell us a little bit what is this special line?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know - but I didn't work in the technical service that maintained the lines, so I may not be the most competent person to provide these explanations. But as far as I know it was a closed system used by the ministry. Speaking about the CSB of Banja Luka, those were leased lines; they were leased from the post office. And it was something like an Intranet [Realtime translation read in error "Internet"], if we used today's terms, a closed network that we would use but which consisted of postal lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe the witness said, 62, 19, "Intranet."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Not "Internet."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that, too. Yes. Internet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you can see the document displayed on the screen, Mr. Raljic. Are you familiar with the system that is diagrammed on the document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen this schematic before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And the title here says that it is the special internal telephone network. Is this the special line that you were talking to us about just now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And this is the pre-war scheme; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just to be clear, after the split of the MUP, you were still able to use this special line?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: For a while, I think we were only able to work within the CSB of Banja Luka, not beyond. But how long exactly, I'm not sure. It was a brief period, but the lines were interrupted and then didn't function anymore. For what reasons, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So you're telling us that it was -- the lines were restricted within the CSB Banja Luka region for a little while?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a very short period. I heard that communications didn't function in other CSBs. I believe that it -- we were able to communicate for a bit longer, but I cannot be specific as to when exactly the lines were interrupted, in which month.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: After the 11th of June, was that line working between Kotor Varos and Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, for the following ten days or so, communication wasn't possible. No lines were in function, not even the -- these special lines. Whether it started functioning again after the 11th [as interpreted] or 25th of June, I -- that -- I'm not privy to that information. I'm not sure. There may have been a couple of calls, but I really don't remember. At the very beginning, it was mostly Miroslav Kalamanda who worked in the duty officers' office, and so it was him who was there mostly, and I cannot be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 63, 20, the witness said "20th or 25th of June," and it was recorded "11th."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I heard that, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, when the lines were -- when the special line was functioning, how easy was it for you to contact Banja Luka? How many codes did have you to type, or how many digits did you have to? Digits.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: It was very simple. You press a button on the phone to be connected to the special line, and, as far as I remember, you only had to dial three digits, possibly four, but I think it was three.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you dialled those three digits, where does it take you to? Let's say you're calling Banja Luka with those three digits, who answers on the other side?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: The operator at the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And that operator would then forward the call to the person that is intended to be called?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was the police chief, Mr. Tepic, using this line to contact his superiors in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you told us that there was also a fax in the police chief [sic]. You told us that there was a dispatch system. If those don't work, is there any other means to transmit information to your superiors? And when I'm talking about your superiors, I'm talking about Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: The only other way was to send the communication by courier, that is, give it to a driver who would then take it away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, in 1992, was a courier system used in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Even before that. And it's used even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And could you tell us what is the distance between Kotor Varos and Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: 30-odd kilometres, approximately. 32, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, to your knowledge, how often would a courier go to Banja Luka from Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: The courier carries regular mail once to twice a week at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, to your knowledge, has it ever occurred that, if you were not able to send a dispatch, that the courier service was used instead?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember any particular instance of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Fair enough. Maybe if I explain the processing of dispatches, that might clarify a little bit. In your section, what was your main role when you are receiving a dispatch from one of the sections of the police station? How do you process it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: There is a procedure in place for receiving and sending dispatches. Upon receiving a dispatch at the communications centre, that dispatch had to contain all prescribed elements. If it didn't, we would place a remark that the dispatch has to be amended. Upon reception of the dispatch, we would check it, whether it contains all these elements. Then we would type it on the teletype machine, and forward it, if it was an open dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, when a dispatch reaches your unit, you told us that you would check whether it contained all the elements. What elements would you look for on a document before dispatching it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: The heading of the dispatch which had to contain the designation of the sender, the number of dispatch, the date, the urgency and confidentiality classification, who it is being sent to, and possible a reference if it refers to another dispatch, as well as the signature of the sender.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You told us about the number of the dispatch. Would you assign that number, or was is somebody else who assigned the number of the dispatch?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Other services would assign a number, those who sent the dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, physically, who would bring down the dispatch to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Usually it was the girl who worked on -- in the administration, a clerical person. But sometimes people from other departments would bring in dispatches, such as the crime police or the regular police. There have been such instances too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And each of these departments, did they have their own coding system, or did it go through a central numbering system?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What do you mean "coding system"? You probably mean something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Let's look at a document and maybe we can have an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we pull up, please -- Your Honours, this is a document that is not on the Prosecution's 65 ter list, but I will just use it for illustration purposes, and I will not seek to tender it. Just to understand the numbering system. The number is 10392. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the top of this document, it says "SJB Kotor Varos." And then we see right below that the dispatch number. Can you explain to us, first of all, the first part, 11-9. What does that represent?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the designation of the organisational unit, namely, the SJB of Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Then we have a backslash and we see 01. What does the 01 represent?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes, 01 stands for the organisational unit within the SJB. Here, it's the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: When you mean "it's the police," which section is that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: I mean the uniformed police and under the commander of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And then we see the number 383. What does that represent?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: It stands for the entry number in the log-book where this dispatch is registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And which log-book would this number come from? To whom did that log-book belong to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: It usually belongs to the entire SJB, and it sits in the office of the administrative service. However, some services have their own log-books, so they can enter the number of their own organisational unit. So I cannot say right now whether this refers to the entire administrative service of the SJB or only that section which belongings to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So what you're telling us is you're not sure if 383 belongs to the log-book of the general police or whether it belongs to the entire police station?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: No, you didn't understand me. If we have this prefix 01, it means that this belongings to the police. It means that this dispatch came from the organisational unit of the police. But this following number, 383, means that they gave this dispatch to the administration for the girl to register it and she would assign a number. Likewise, they could enter their own number from the -- the log-book of that subordinate unit. This 383 may be a -- an enter number in the log-book that belonged to the entire SJB.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just to be clear, 383 is a sequential number; does it start from 1 at the beginning of the year?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the usual situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We can put that document away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in terms of log-books, did your section have log-books?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: How many log-books did you have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: We had one for sending and transmitting open-type dispatches, so we had two books: One for sending and one for transmitting. And then we had two: One for sending and one for receiving encoded dispatches.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And -- so that would be four log-books. Are these log-books still in existence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: No, they're not in existence anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What happens to these log-books?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: These log-books are kept for a period of up to five years, according to the regulations applying to communications and encoding service, these log-books are kept for a period of five years, after which they are destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And how about the dispatches? How long did you keep the dispatches?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: In principle, the communications centre does not keep the dispatches. After sending a dispatch, we keep it for another 24 hours for the case of some problems detected by the receiving side, if the printout was poor or something like that, so that we could re-send it. And after 24 hours, we returned the dispatch to the sender. We were not filing the dispatches themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And how about incoming dispatches?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Incoming dispatches were submitted to those who they were addressed to, depending on the priority level. In our case, we were sending or forwarding the dispatches to the chief of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, when a dispatch comes in, and let's say it is addressed to the head of the crime service, you just told us that you would forward the dispatches to the chief of the public security. Did all of them go to him first, or did you direct it to -- let's say, the head of crime service in this example?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. No, in principle all the dispatches would be forwarded to the chief of the public security station who would review them, and then, having done that, he would, at the bottom of the dispatch, designate who should be getting this dispatch and acting upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, we saw one dispatch earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we can display a second one, which is 10393. This one, too, Your Honours, I will not seek to tender it. It is not on our 65 ter list. But just for illustration purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, the first we saw was dated the 1st of August, 1992. This one is the 12th of September, 1992. And right after the 11-9, what number can you see there?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we can maybe zoom into that section up there, the top left-hand corner. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After 11-9, we can see 09-387 [Realtime transcript read in error "01"] forward slash 92.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, I'm sorry, it says "01" in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: After the 11-9, what do you have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Number 09 at the time was organisational unit called Administration and Legal Section of the SJB. And then number 387 is most probably the number in the log-book where it was entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, having been in Kotor Varos yourself in -- in August and September 1992, let me ask you the following: We see 09-387, and on the previous document we saw 01-383. Now, there's only four numbers of difference within a month and a half. From that, are you able to tell us whether the sequence of numbers was given by each section or whether it was given by a general section?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, it is possible that -- that the number was off the general section -- or, rather, the administration section, but some of the services had their own log-books. Now, I cannot tell you about there specific number, 387, but my guess would be that this is this general section number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we could display on the screen 65 ter 3195, which is tab 11 on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to show you a report which appears to be a -- a report of the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you see a document on your screen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... tab?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Tab 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise the document. This is a yearly report or annual report on organisation and work of the KZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. It says KZ in the transcript. Do you mean communication and cryptography by that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes, cryptography.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, who drafted this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: I drafted this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This, you said, is an annual report. First, before we look at this document, were there other reports you sent periodically throughout the year?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Usually the reports were and are sent monthly, but they would only cover the traffic of dispatches.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we can turn to -- if can go to the bottom of the first page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We can see the first paragraph here seems to give a historic of your section, with a description of the staff members. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And we see here that it talks about Mr. Kalamanda, who you mentioned earlier. And it mentions that you joined in November 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And if we turn to the second page in the English version and in the B/C/S version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We can see that it talks about Mr. Popovic, you mentioned earlier, who was hired that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we can go to the third page, both in English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We see, at the bottom of that page, the numbers of telegrams that were sent and received throughout that year. And does that -- is that an accurate description of the situation during that year?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's an accurate description of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And it says here that you received 2530 open dispatches, you received 150 encrypted dispatches, and you sent 837 open dispatches, and you sent 21 encrypted dispatches. Now, I would like to understand the number 837 of sent open dispatches. Can you tell us what kind of dispatches would be sent open?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: All dispatches that did not contain, to put it briefly, any secret information were sent by open dispatch system. For instance, whether there was need for some equipment, if someone from the political structures was passing through Kotor Varos and needed escort through town; whereas, dispatches which required any degree of secrecy were not sent through this open system.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And if we can go to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And I would ask to you look at the last paragraphs. It reads here that: "All communication and cryptographic protection affairs in the SJB Kotor Varos are conducted successfully and without major difficulties considering the current situation." Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do see the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So to come back to what you told us earlier. In the initial seven to ten days you were having problems. This -- your conclusion for the year is despite the difficulties you are able to send dispatches. Is that -- and if that's correct, can you tell us, roughly speaking, when it is that the situation allowed you to send dispatches?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: The situation became relatively normal, although it never became fully normal in the few years to come, but relatively normal. It was as of the end of the year onwards. As you said in the last paragraph, we can see that considering the current situation it's conducted successfully. So it means at the time of reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask for this document to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I have one last, short topic before we --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise. This will be Exhibit P1486, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I just have an observation, Your Honours. I believe it might be important. This document --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honours, that the English translation that -- does not correspond entirely to the Serbian original. Because -- and that is exactly what witness was explaining, and I don't know if it's clear to Your Honours. The English translation uses the -- the Serbian original contains the word "zazada," which means "at this moment." And it's not a part of the English translation. So I think that that is what is creating the difficulty for my learned friend and the witness to comment on the document because the English translation does not -- does not contain that particular part of the original. So I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The witness concluded that he was at the time of reporting, so I think that clarifies the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But the officially translation should contain everything which is in the original. And we need to -- to re-send it for verification of translation. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'll look into it. Very well. One last topic before we resume [sic] for the day, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Raljic, you were telling us about the courier system. I'd like to ask you about the SJB chief, Mr. Tepic, himself. Would he attend meetings with his superiors?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The chief would attend meetings with his superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And this is in Banja Luka; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was in the CS -- or, CJB [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, how often, to your knowledge, would Mr. Tepic go to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: During which period?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'm talking about the year 1992.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: Chief Tepic, in 1992, would relatively frequently go there. Initially - and we are discussing the meetings now - initially, if they had a collegium which was scheduled and announced through dispatches and they would hold a meeting, they would have an agenda for the chiefs to prepare for the discussion and their briefings, and then after the 11th of June, I don't remember receiving any dispatches announcing a meeting of the collegium. But the chief would travel often. I think, on the average, two or three times a week. Now, whether he was on these occasions going to the centre or was he going to do some private business of his, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And during the first part of the year 1992, do you know who his driver was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: During the first part of 1992, I was the driver, the chief's driver. And then after the April of 1992, there were two other guys who would alternate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, generally speaking, when you drove the chief, where did you drive him to in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: If we would be going to the public security centre, then I would take him to the public security centre -- or, rather, sometimes we would go to Laktasi or other locations in Banja Luka. The chief was not strictly using his official vehicle only to go to the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And one last question on this topic: When he would attend the meetings at Banja Luka, who would have called for those meetings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC
utterances.text: As I mentioned, these meetings would be announced, we would receive dispatches to that effect, and the meetings were convened by the chief of the CSB, Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It may be a good time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. It is the time when we would take the adjournment for today. I would remind Mr. Raljic, the witness, that having been sworn as a witness, that you cannot communicate with counsel from either side until you are released, and such conversations that you have outside the Chamber, you cannot discuss your testimony. So we adjourn, to reconvene tomorrow in this courtroom at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 30th day of June, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.
